Cost of Capital: WACC Formula, Cost of Debt and Cost of Equity

The cost of capital is the minimum return a company must earn to keep its lenders and shareholders satisfied. It is the discount rate in capital budgeting and valuation, and this guide works it out step by step.

2 min readFor MBA, BBA and BBMUpdated 2 November 2026

Cost of debt

After-tax cost of debt = interest rate × (1 − tax rate). A 10% loan at a 25% tax rate costs 10% × 0.75 = 7.5%.

Interest is tax-deductible, and so debt is cheaper than it first looks. Dividends on equity do not get this benefit.

Cost of equity

Equity has no stated rate, so it must be estimated from what shareholders expect. There are two standard methods.

  • CAPM: cost of equity = risk-free rate + beta × market risk premium. With a 7% risk-free rate, a beta of 1.2 and a 5% premium, it is 13%.
  • Dividend growth (Gordon) model: cost of equity = next year's dividend ÷ share price + growth. With a ₹5 dividend, a ₹100 price and 8% growth, it is 5% + 8% = 13%.

Cost of preference shares

Cost of preference capital = preference dividend ÷ net proceeds. A share issued for ₹98 net, paying ₹9 a year, costs 9 ÷ 98 = 9.18%. There is no tax adjustment, because the dividend is not deductible.

WACC: a worked example

WACC weights each source of finance by its share in the company's capital, ideally using market values.

SourceWeightCost after taxWeighted cost
Equity60%13.0%7.8%
Debt40%7.5%3.0%
WACC100%10.8%

WACC = (E/V × cost of equity) + (D/V × cost of debt × (1 − tax rate)).

A project earning above 10.8% with risk like the company's adds value; one earning less destroys it. A project far riskier than the company's normal business should use a higher rate.

Why more debt is not always cheaper

Debt costs less than equity, so adding some can lower WACC. But more debt raises the risk of financial distress, and then both lenders and shareholders demand more. This is why there is said to be an optimal capital structure, a question we take up in our guide on leverage.

Exam and interview questions

Why is debt usually cheaper than equity?

Lenders have a prior claim and a contractual return, so they accept less, and interest is also tax-deductible.

Should WACC use book or market weights?

Market weights are preferred, because they reflect what investors would need to be paid today. Book weights are often used in exams when market data is not given.

Why is the cost of equity not zero if a company pays no dividend?

Because shareholders still expect a return, through price rises. Retained profit belongs to them, and has an opportunity cost.
